docs.title: EvalSuite
docs.text:
Unified, reproducible evaluation for machine learning and research — every metric with a confidence interval.

pip install evalsuite-python

import evalsuite as es

result = es.evaluate(y_true, y_pred, y_prob=y_prob)
print(result.summary())
  • Guides live in the README.
  • API reference: see the sections in the navigation, generated from the docstrings of this version.
  • Stability: see the deprecation policy.

docs.title: Stability and deprecation policy
docs.text:
EvalSuite follows semantic versioning from 2.0.0 on.

  • Patch releases (2.0.x) fix bugs. They never change a public name or signature, and they never change a result unless the old result was wrong (the changelog says so under Fixed).
  • Minor releases (2.x.0) add features. Existing code keeps working and keeps producing the same numbers.
  • Major releases (3.0.0) may remove or change public API, but only after a deprecation period.

Public API means every name in evalsuite.__all__, the command-line interface, and the documented keyword arguments. Names starting with _ are private and may change at any time.

Deprecation. A feature to be removed first emits a DeprecationWarning (category EvalSuiteDeprecationWarning) naming its replacement, for at least two minor releases and at least six months, and is listed under Deprecated in the changelog. It is removed only in the next major release.

Results. Default settings (resample counts, interval methods, random-number streams) are part of the contract: changing one so that results move is treated as a breaking change, unless it fixes a bug. Seeded results (random_state=) are reproducible across platforms and between the compiled core and pure Python.

Supported versions. The latest minor release receives fixes; security fixes go to the latest two minor releases. Python versions follow NumPy's support window.

docs.title: evalsuite.calibration
docs.text:
Calibration of predicted probabilities: maximum calibration error, calibration slope and intercept (logistic recalibration) and the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test.

The calibration curve, expected calibration error and Brier score live in :mod:evalsuite.classification and are re-exported here for convenience.

docs.title: hosmer_lemeshow
docs.text:
hosmer_lemeshow(y_true: ArrayLike, y_prob: ArrayLike, *, n_groups: int = 10, pos_label: Any = None) -> TestResult

Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test for predicted risks.

Observations are sorted by predicted risk and split into n_groups groups of (nearly) equal size ("deciles of risk"). The statistic Σ (O − E)² / (E (1 − E/nₖ)) is compared with χ² on n_groups − 2 degrees of freedom (use n_groups degrees of freedom for an external validation set by reading params["statistic"]). A large p-value does not show that calibration is good, especially in small samples; report the calibration curve, slope and intercept as well.

docs.title: evalsuite.recalibration
docs.text:
Recalibration: fit a map from a model's probabilities to calibrated ones on held-out data, then apply it.

import evalsuite as es cal = es.recalibrate(y_val, p_val, method="isotonic") # "platt", "temperature", "beta", "histogram" p_test_cal = cal(p_test) # or cal.transform(p_test) es.calibration_report(y_test, p_test_cal, n_resamples=1000) # check it on separate data, with CIs

Methods: Platt scaling (Platt 1999, with Platt's smoothed targets, on the logit of the probabilities), isotonic regression (Zadrozny & Elkan 2002; pool-adjacent-violators, clipped outside the fitted range), temperature scaling (Guo et al. 2017; one parameter, also for multiclass probability matrices), beta calibration (Kull, Silva Filho & Flach 2017; three parameters) and histogram binning (equal-mass bins). Fit on data the model was not trained on, and evaluate on different data again.

docs.title: evalsuite.conformal
docs.text:
Conformal prediction: prediction sets and intervals with a finite-sample coverage guarantee.

import evalsuite as es sets = es.conformal_classification(y_cal, p_cal, p_test, alpha=0.1) # 90% prediction sets sets.sets[0], sets.mean_size es.conformal_classification(y_cal, p_cal, p_test, y_test=y_test).coverage # check on labelled data iv = es.conformal_regression(y_cal, yhat_cal, yhat_test, alpha=0.1) # 90% intervals iv.lower, iv.upper

Split conformal prediction (Vovk et al. 2005; Lei et al. 2018; Angelopoulos & Bates 2023): a held-out calibration set gives the score threshold q̂ = the ⌈(n + 1)(1 − α)⌉-th smallest calibration score, and for a new exchangeable example P(y ∈ set) ≥ 1 − α, whatever the model. Classification scores: "lac" (1 − probability of the true class; smallest sets), "aps" (adaptive prediction sets, Romano et al. 2020; sets that grow with uncertainty) and "raps" (regularised APS, Angelopoulos et al. 2021). Regression: "absolute" residuals, "normalized" residuals divided by a per-example scale (e.g. a predicted SD) and "cqr" (conformalized quantile regression, Romano et al. 2019) from lower / upper quantile predictions. by= gives Mondrian (group-conditional) conformal prediction: a threshold per group, so coverage holds within every group (classes, sites, subgroups).

With labelled test data, the result reports empirical coverage with a Wilson interval, the coverage per group and per set size, and set sizes / interval widths — the checks reviewers ask for.

docs.title: conformal_regression
docs.text:
conformal_regression(y_cal: Any, pred_cal: Any, pred_test: Any, *, alpha: float = 0.1, method: str = 'absolute', scale_cal: Any = None, scale_test: Any = None, y_test: Any = None, by: Any = None, by_test: Any = None, level: float = 0.95) -> ConformalIntervals

Split-conformal prediction intervals (see the module docstring).

"absolute": pred_* are point predictions; interval pred ± q̂. "normalized": also give scale_cal / scale_test (positive per-example scales such as predicted SDs); interval pred ± q̂·scale. "cqr": pred_* are n × 2 arrays of lower and upper quantile predictions (e.g. the α/2 and 1 − α/2 quantiles); interval [lo − q̂, hi + q̂]. by / by_test give a threshold per group.

docs.title: evalsuite.classification.metrics
docs.text:
Classification metrics for binary, multiclass and multilabel targets.

Conventions (stated once, applied everywhere):

  • labels order defines per-class outputs and the columns of 2-D y_prob. By default it is the sorted set of labels present in y_true and y_pred.
  • average="auto" means "binary" for binary targets and "macro" otherwise; the resolved value is recorded in result.params["average"].
  • Undefined ratios (zero denominators) follow zero_division: "warn" returns 0 with an :class:~evalsuite.core.exceptions.UndefinedMetricWarning; np.nan propagates NaN.

Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratio, Youden's J, accuracy and prevalence for a binary test, each with a confidence interval.

Intervals: proportions use proportion_method (Wilson by default, or "clopper-pearson"); likelihood ratios use the log method of Simel et al. (1991); the diagnostic odds ratio uses Woolf's log method with 0.5 added to every cell when one is zero; Youden's J uses the Wald interval from the independent sensitivity and specificity variances, clipped to [−1, 1].

docs.title: evalsuite.survival
docs.text:
Time-to-event (survival) evaluation with right-censored data.

  • :func:concordance_index — Harrell's C (ipcw=False) or Uno's IPCW C (ipcw=True), with a bootstrap interval on request.
  • :func:time_dependent_auc — cumulative/dynamic ROC AUC at each time point (Uno et al. 2007; Hung & Chiang 2010), and its mean over time.
  • :func:brier_score_survival / :func:integrated_brier_score — Graf et al. (1999) IPCW Brier score at each time point and integrated over a time range.
  • :func:kaplan_meier — the Kaplan–Meier estimate (and of the censoring distribution, reverse=True).

Conventions follow scikit-survival, and the results agree with it (tests in tests/test_survival.py): event is True / 1 for an observed event and False / 0 for censoring; risk is a risk score (higher means earlier events); survival-probability estimate columns correspond to times. Inverse-probability-of- censoring weights come from the Kaplan–Meier estimate of the censoring distribution fitted on train_time / train_event (default: the evaluation data).

docs.title: SurvivalCurve dataclass
docs.text: A step function: prob[k] holds from time[k] until the next time point.

docs.title: kaplan_meier
docs.text:
kaplan_meier(time: Any, event: Any, *, reverse: bool = False) -> SurvivalCurve

Kaplan–Meier survival curve; reverse=True estimates the censoring distribution G(t) (at tied times, events leave the risk set before censorings, as in scikit-survival).

docs.title: concordance_index
docs.text:
concordance_index(time: Any, event: Any, risk: Any, *, ipcw: bool = False, tau: Optional[float] = None, train_time: Any = None, train_event: Any = None, tied_tol: float = 1e-08, ci: Optional[str] = None, level: float = 0.95, n_resamples: int = 1000, random_state: Optional[int] = 0) -> MetricResult

Concordance index for risk scores: the share of comparable pairs whose higher-risk member fails first (ties in risk count 1/2). ipcw=False: Harrell's C. ipcw=True: Uno's C, pairs weighted by 1 / G(t_i)² (censoring KM from train_*), optionally truncated at tau. ci="bootstrap" adds a percentile interval over resampled subjects.

docs.title: time_dependent_auc
docs.text:
time_dependent_auc(time: Any, event: Any, risk: Any, times: Any, *, train_time: Any = None, train_event: Any = None, tied_tol: float = 1e-08) -> MetricResult

Cumulative/dynamic AUC at each of times: how well the risk scores separate subjects with an event by time t (cases, IPCW-weighted) from those still event-free after t (controls). risk is one score per subject or one column per time point. value is the mean AUC weighted by the Kaplan–Meier drop over the times; params["auc"] the per-time values.

docs.title: brier_score_survival
docs.text:
brier_score_survival(time: Any, event: Any, estimate: Any, times: Any, *, train_time: Any = None, train_event: Any = None) -> MetricResult

IPCW Brier score (Graf et al. 1999) of predicted survival probabilities estimate[:, k] = P(T > times[k]) at each time point; value is the mean over times, params["brier"] the per-time values.

docs.title: integrated_brier_score
docs.text:
integrated_brier_score(time: Any, event: Any, estimate: Any, times: Any, *, train_time: Any = None, train_event: Any = None) -> MetricResult

Integrated Brier score: the IPCW Brier score integrated over times (trapezoidal rule) and divided by the time range. Needs at least two time points. Lower is better; 0.25 is the score of predicting 0.5.

docs.title: evalsuite.reclassification
docs.text:
Clinical model updates: does a new risk model reclassify patients better, and does a model transport to a new site?

import evalsuite as es es.reclassification(y, p_old, p_new, cutoffs=[0.05, 0.2]) # NRI (categorical and continuous) and IDI es.external_validation(y_dev, p_dev, y_ext, p_ext) # development vs external site, and recalibration

Net reclassification improvement (Pencina et al., Stat Med 2008): among events, the share moved to a higher risk category minus the share moved lower; among non-events, the share moved lower minus higher; the NRI is their sum. The continuous (category-free) NRI counts any increase or decrease (Pencina et al. 2011). The integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) is the gain in mean predicted risk among events minus that among non-events. P-values use Pencina's asymptotic z tests; intervals are percentile bootstrap (paired, stratified by outcome).

external_validation reports discrimination (DeLong CIs and the unpaired difference), calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, observed / expected ratio and Brier score at both sites, and how much intercept-only and logistic recalibration on the external data would recover (Steyerberg, Clinical Prediction Models, ch. 19).

docs.text: NRI (categorical and continuous) and IDI with p-values and bootstrap intervals.

docs.title: ExternalValidation dataclass
docs.text: Performance at the development and the external site, and what recalibration would recover.

NRI and IDI of a new risk model against an old one on the same patients (see the module docstring). cutoffs (e.g. [0.05, 0.2]) define risk categories for the categorical NRI and the reclassification tables; the continuous NRI and the IDI are always reported.

docs.title: evalsuite.cards
docs.text:
Reporting standards: the evaluation sections that journals and model cards ask for, generated from data.

report_card(y_true, y_prob, standard="tripod-ai") computes what TRIPOD+AI (Collins et al., BMJ 2024) asks a prediction-model paper to report about performance (sample size and outcome events; discrimination; calibration in the large, slope and plot-free summaries; classification at a threshold; clinical utility by net benefit; performance in subgroups) with confidence intervals, writes it up as a results paragraph and a table, and lists which checklist items are covered and which need your own text. standard="stard" (STARD 2015, diagnostic accuracy studies) and standard="consort-ai" (CONSORT-AI, trials of AI interventions) fill in those checklists' results items the same way. standard="model-card" produces the sections of a model card (Mitchell et al., FAT* 2019) with the quantitative analyses filled in and the narrative sections taken from context.

Export with to_markdown(), to_latex(), to_html() or to_docx(path) (python-docx).

A results paragraph in the style of a methods/results section.

docs.title: report_card
docs.text:
report_card(y_true: Any, y_prob: Any, *, y_pred: Any = None, standard: str = 'tripod-ai', threshold: float = 0.5, groups: Optional[Sequence[Any]] = None, group_name: str = 'subgroup', context: Optional[Mapping[str, str]] = None, pos_label: Any = None, level: float = 0.95, n_resamples: int = 1000, random_state: Optional[int] = 0) -> ReportCard

Performance section for a reporting standard ("tripod-ai", "stard" for diagnostic accuracy studies, "consort-ai" for trials of AI interventions, or "model-card") from a binary outcome and predicted risks. groups adds a subgroup (fairness) table; context supplies the narrative sections of a model card (keys: model_details, intended_use, factors, metrics, evaluation_data, training_data, ethical_considerations, caveats). Intervals: DeLong for ROC AUC, Wilson for proportions, bootstrap (seeded) for calibration and the Brier score.

docs.title: evalsuite.fairness
docs.text:
Fairness: performance by group, gaps between groups with confidence intervals, and corrected tests.

fairness_report(y_true, y_pred, y_prob, groups=...) reports, for every group (and every intersection of several attributes), the selection rate, true and false positive rates, positive predictive value and accuracy (Wilson intervals), plus ROC AUC (DeLong) and calibration-in-the-large with probabilities. It then gives the standard gap measures with bootstrap intervals that resample within each group:

  • demographic parity difference (max − min selection rate) and ratio (min / max, the "four-fifths rule"),
  • equalized odds difference (the larger of the TPR and FPR gaps; Hardt et al. 2016),
  • equal opportunity difference (TPR gap) and predictive parity difference (PPV gap),

and tests every group against a reference group (Fisher's exact test per metric, Holm-adjusted across all tests). Groups smaller than min_group_size are listed but not tested. The gap definitions match Fairlearn's.

docs.title: FairnessReport dataclass
docs.text: Per-group metrics, gap measures and tests (see :func:fairness_report).

docs.title: fairness_report
docs.text:
fairness_report(y_true: Any, y_pred: Any = None, y_prob: Any = None, *, groups: Union[Mapping[str, Any], Sequence[Any], ndarray], pos_label: Any = 1, threshold: float = 0.5, reference: Optional[str] = None, intersectional: bool = True, min_group_size: int = 10, level: float = 0.95, alpha: float = 0.05, n_resamples: int = 1000, random_state: Optional[int] = 0) -> FairnessReport

Group fairness of a binary classifier.

groups: one protected-attribute value per observation, or a mapping of attribute name → values (several attributes are crossed into intersectional groups such as sex=F & age=65+; with intersectional=False each attribute is analysed on its own and the reports' groups are listed per attribute). y_pred gives labels; with only y_prob labels are y_prob >= threshold. reference: the group the others are tested against (default: the largest).

docs.title: evalsuite.comparisons
docs.text:
Comparisons beyond "is there a difference": equivalence and non-inferiority, many models over many data sets, and metrics when some labels are missing.

import evalsuite as es es.noninferiority_test("accuracy", y, pred_new, pred_old, margin=0.02) # is the new model no worse? es.equivalence_test("roc_auc", y, y_prob_a=pa, y_prob_b=pb, margin=0.01) # practically the same (TOST)? nem = es.nemenyi_test(scores) # datasets × models → average ranks, critical difference, pairwise p es.plot.critical_difference(nem) # the critical-difference diagram (Demšar 2006) es.ipw_metric("accuracy", y, pred, observed=has_label, p_observed=propensity)

Non-inferiority and equivalence follow the FDA / EMA two one-sided tests (TOST, Schuirmann 1987) on the paired bootstrap distribution of metric(A) − metric(B): non-inferior when the lower (1 − 2α) bound exceeds −margin; equivalent when the whole (1 − 2α) interval lies inside ±margin. The Nemenyi test (Nemenyi 1963; Demšar, JMLR 2006) compares every pair of models by average rank across data sets after a Friedman test. ipw_metric weights labelled examples by the inverse probability of having a label (Horvitz–Thompson), which removes the bias of evaluating only on cases that happened to be labelled when labelling depends on observed covariates.

docs.title: NemenyiResult dataclass
docs.text: Friedman test, average ranks, critical difference and pairwise Nemenyi p-values.

docs.title: noninferiority_test
docs.text:
noninferiority_test(metric: Any, y_true: Any, y_pred_a: Any = None, y_pred_b: Any = None, *, margin: float, alpha: float = 0.025, y_prob_a: Any = None, y_prob_b: Any = None, sample_weight: Any = None, higher_is_better: Optional[bool] = None, n_resamples: int = 2000, random_state: Optional[int] = None, stratify: Optional[bool] = None, **metric_kwargs: Any) -> TestResult

Is model A (new) no worse than model B (reference) by more than margin? One-sided test at alpha (0.025 by default, as regulators expect) on paired bootstrap differences; params["conclusion"] is True when the lower (1 − 2α) confidence bound of A − B (oriented so higher is better) is above −margin.

docs.title: equivalence_test
docs.text:
equivalence_test(metric: Any, y_true: Any, y_pred_a: Any = None, y_pred_b: Any = None, *, margin: float, alpha: float = 0.05, y_prob_a: Any = None, y_prob_b: Any = None, sample_weight: Any = None, n_resamples: int = 2000, random_state: Optional[int] = None, stratify: Optional[bool] = None, **metric_kwargs: Any) -> TestResult

Are models A and B equivalent within ±margin? Two one-sided tests (TOST) at alpha on paired bootstrap differences; params["conclusion"] is True when the (1 − 2α) interval of A − B lies inside ±margin.

docs.title: nemenyi_test
docs.text:
nemenyi_test(scores: Any, *, models: Optional[list[str]] = None, alpha: float = 0.05, higher_is_better: bool = True) -> NemenyiResult

Compare k models over N data sets (or folds): scores is N × k (a DataFrame's columns name the models), or a mapping model → N scores. Ranks are computed per data set (ties share the average rank; 1 = best).

docs.title: ipw_metric
docs.text:
ipw_metric(metric: Any, y_true: Any, y_pred: Any = None, *, observed: Any, p_observed: Any, y_prob: Any = None, clip: Union[float, tuple[float, float]] = 0.01, **metric_kwargs: Any) -> MetricResult

A metric over the whole population when only some examples are labelled: labelled examples (observed True) are weighted by 1 / p_observed (their estimated probability of being labelled, e.g. from a logistic model of labelling on covariates). Propensities are clipped to [clip, 1] to limit extreme weights. params reports the effective sample size and the unweighted (complete-case) value for comparison.

docs.title: evalsuite.agreement
docs.text:
Agreement studies: how well raters, instruments or methods agree on the same subjects.

import evalsuite as es icc = es.icc(ratings) # subjects × raters matrix → all six ICC forms with CIs icc["ICC2"].value, icc["ICC2"].low, icc["ICC2"].high ba = es.bland_altman(method_a, method_b) # bias, limits of agreement (with CIs), proportional bias ccc = es.lins_ccc(method_a, method_b) # Lin's concordance correlation with a CI

ICC forms follow Shrout & Fleiss (1979) and McGraw & Wong (1996), with the exact F-based confidence intervals (ICC2 by Satterthwaite's approximation), as in pingouin and R's psych::ICC. Bland–Altman limits use the Bland & Altman (1999) standard errors; Lin's CCC uses the Fisher-z interval of Lin (1989).

docs.text: One intraclass correlation: estimate, F test against zero and confidence interval.

docs.text: All six ICC forms for a subjects × raters table. Index by form name (result["ICC2"]).

icc(ratings: Any, *, subjects: Any = None, raters: Any = None, level: float = 0.95, missing: str = 'drop') -> ICCResult

Intraclass correlation coefficients (all six Shrout–Fleiss forms) with F tests and confidence intervals.

ratings is a subjects × raters table, or one rating per row with subjects= and raters= (long format). Subjects with a missing rating are dropped (missing="drop") or rejected (missing="raise"). Choose the form by design: ICC2 / ICC2k when the raters are a sample of possible raters and absolute agreement matters, ICC3 / ICC3k for these fixed raters' consistency, ICC1 when each subject has different raters; "k" forms describe the mean of the k ratings.

docs.title: evalsuite.bayes
docs.text:
Bayesian comparison of two models: the probability that one is better, not a p-value.

import evalsuite as es b = es.bayes_compare(y_true, pred_a, pred_b, metric="accuracy", rope=0.01) b.p_a_better, b.p_rope, b.p_b_better # probabilities that sum to 1 b.summary() # "A is better with probability 0.97 ..." es.bayes_correlated_ttest(cv_scores_a, cv_scores_b, test_fraction=0.2, rope=0.01)

bayes_compare puts a Bayesian bootstrap (Rubin 1981: flat Dirichlet weights over the test examples) on the paired test set and returns the posterior of the metric difference, its credible interval and the probabilities of A better, practically equivalent (inside the region of practical equivalence, ROPE) and B better. bayes_correlated_ttest is the correlated Bayesian t-test of Benavoli et al. (2017) for scores from k-fold cross-validation, where training sets overlap.

docs.title: bayes_compare
docs.text:
bayes_compare(y_true: Any, pred_a: Any, pred_b: Any, *, metric: Union[str, Callable[..., Any]] = 'accuracy', rope: Union[float, tuple[float, float]] = 0.01, level: float = 0.95, n_samples: int = 4000, higher_is_better: Optional[bool] = None, random_state: Optional[int] = None, **metric_kwargs: Any) -> BayesComparison

Posterior of the difference in metric between two models scored on the same examples.

Each posterior draw weights the test examples by flat Dirichlet weights (Bayesian bootstrap) and evaluates the metric on both models with those weights, so the pairing is kept. pred_a / pred_b are labels, or scores for probability metrics (metric="roc_auc", "brier"...). rope is the region of practical equivalence on the metric's scale (±0.01 by default).

docs.title: bayes_correlated_ttest
docs.text:
bayes_correlated_ttest(scores_a: Any, scores_b: Any, *, test_fraction: Optional[float] = None, rope: Union[float, tuple[float, float]] = 0.01, level: float = 0.95, higher_is_better: bool = True, n_samples: int = 50000, random_state: Optional[int] = None, metric: str = 'score') -> BayesComparison

Correlated Bayesian t-test (Benavoli, Corani, Demšar & Zaffalon 2017) for per-fold cross-validation scores of two models on the same folds. test_fraction is n_test / n_total of a fold (1/k for k-fold; the default), which sets the correlation between folds (Nadeau & Bengio 2003). The posterior of the mean difference is a Student t with n − 1 degrees of freedom; probabilities are exact and the draws only feed samples.

docs.title: evaluate
docs.text:
evaluate(y_true: ArrayLike, y_pred: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, *, y_prob: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, task: Optional[str] = None, metrics: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, average: Optional[str] = 'auto', labels: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, pos_label: Any = None, sample_weight: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, zero_division: ZeroDivision = 'warn', ci: Any = 'analytic', level: float = 0.95, baseline_pred: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, baseline_prob: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, n_resamples: int = 1000, random_state: Optional[int] = 0, clusters: Optional[ArrayLike] = None) -> EvaluationResult

Evaluate predictions with a standard set of metrics (or the metrics you name), with confidence intervals and, given a baseline, paired significance tests against it.

The task is inferred when omitted: probabilities or integer/string labels mean classification, non-integer numbers mean regression. Inputs are validated once and shared intermediate results (the confusion matrix) are computed once for all metrics.

import evalsuite as es r = es.evaluate([0, 1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 0, 0]) round(r["accuracy"], 2) 0.75

Intervals (level, 95% by default) are in each metric's params (ci_low, ci_high, ci_method) and in every summary and export. ci="analytic" (default, no extra cost) gives closed-form intervals where a standard one exists: Wilson for accuracy / precision / recall / specificity / NPV, DeLong for binary ROC AUC, Student-t for mean losses (Brier, log loss, MAE, MSE, RMSE, mean bias). ci="bootstrap" gives paired percentile-bootstrap intervals for every metric (n_resamples, seeded by random_state); ci=False turns them off. baseline_pred / baseline_prob (e.g. the current model) add the difference, its interval and a paired test per metric (McNemar for accuracy, DeLong for ROC AUC, paired bootstrap otherwise; Holm-adjusted), as baseline_* params and result.comparison. clusters (one id per observation, e.g. the patient of each scan or the document of each question) makes every interval and baseline test a cluster bootstrap that resamples whole clusters; ordinary intervals are too narrow when observations within a cluster are correlated.

docs.title: bootstrap_ci
docs.text:
bootstrap_ci(metric: Any, y_true: ArrayLike, y_pred: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, *, y_prob: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, sample_weight: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, level: float = 0.95, method: BootstrapMethod = 'bca', n_resamples: int = 2000, random_state: Optional[int] = None, stratify: Optional[bool] = None, jackknife_groups: int = 1000, resampling: str = 'numpy', clusters: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, **metric_kwargs: Any) -> ConfidenceInterval

Bootstrap confidence interval for any metric.

``metric`` is a metric function (``es.f1``) or its name (``"f1"``). Pass ``y_pred`` for label/value
metrics or ``y_prob`` for probability metrics; extra keyword arguments go to the metric (for example
``average="macro"``). Resampling is stratified by class for classification targets unless
``stratify=False``, so every resample contains every class. For classification metrics that accept
``labels``, the full label set is fixed across resamples.

``method``: ``"bca"`` (bias-corrected and accelerated; default, Efron 1987), ``"percentile"`` or
``"basic"``. Set ``random_state`` for reproducible intervals. Resamples on which the metric is undefined
are counted in ``params["failed_resamples"]``; more than 10% raises :class:`StatisticalTestError`.

resampling="native" (opt-in) draws the resample indices in the compiled core instead of NumPy: faster on large inputs and still reproducible with random_state, but a different random stream from the default.

clusters (one id per observation: patient, document, site, conversation) resamples whole clusters instead of observations (cluster bootstrap; Field & Welsh 2007), so correlated observations in a cluster are kept together. Ordinary intervals are too narrow when observations are clustered; the cluster interval is honest. BCa's acceleration then uses leave-one-cluster-out estimates.

References: Efron B. Better bootstrap confidence intervals. JASA. 1987;82(397):171-185.
Efron B, Tibshirani RJ. An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman & Hall; 1993.

docs.title: cluster_distribution
docs.text:
cluster_distribution(call: MetricCall, members: list[NDArray[int64]], picks: list[NDArray[Any]]) -> tuple[NDArray[np.float64], int]

Metric value on each cluster resample (picks[b] lists the drawn clusters), NaN where undefined.

Equal to concatenating the drawn clusters' observations and calling the metric, but much faster: confusion-matrix metrics add up per-cluster code counts (one small matrix product for all resamples), and binary ROC AUC / average precision weight each observation by how often its cluster was drawn.

docs.title: compare
docs.text:
compare(y_true: ArrayLike, predictions: Optional[Mapping[str, ArrayLike]] = None, *, probabilities: Optional[Mapping[str, ArrayLike]] = None, metrics: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, baseline: Optional[str] = None, level: float = 0.95, alpha: float = 0.05, n_resamples: int = 1000, correction: str = 'holm', random_state: Optional[int] = None, stratify: Optional[bool] = None, sample_weight: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, metric_kwargs: Optional[Mapping[str, Mapping[str, Any]]] = None, resampling: str = 'numpy', _allow_single: bool = False) -> ComparisonResult

Compare models evaluated on the same test set.

predictions and/or probabilities map model names to that model's predicted labels/values or probabilities. Every model is resampled on the same bootstrap indices (paired), giving a percentile confidence interval per model and metric and a paired test per pair of models:

  • accuracy: McNemar's test (exact when there are fewer than 25 discordant pairs);
  • binary ROC AUC: DeLong's test;
  • everything else: paired bootstrap test.

Pairs are every model against baseline if given, otherwise all pairs. p-values are adjusted within each metric (correction: "holm", "bonferroni", "hochberg", "bh", "by"); significant uses the adjusted p-value and alpha. metric_kwargs passes options per metric, e.g. {"f1": {"average": "macro"}}. resampling="native" (opt-in) draws the bootstrap indices in the compiled core; see :func:bootstrap_ci.

docs.title: evalsuite.stats.paired
docs.text: Paired tests for comparing two models evaluated on the same observations.

docs.title: mcnemar_test
docs.text:
mcnemar_test(y_true: ArrayLike, y_pred_a: ArrayLike, y_pred_b: ArrayLike, *, exact: Optional[bool] = None, correction: bool = True) -> TestResult

McNemar's test: do two classifiers have the same error rate on the same observations?

Uses only discordant pairs: b = A right & B wrong, c = A wrong & B right. exact=None (default) uses the exact binomial test when b + c < 25 and the chi-squared test otherwise (with Edwards' continuity correction unless correction=False). estimate is the accuracy difference A − B.

References: McNemar Q. Psychometrika. 1947;12(2):153-157. Edwards AL. Psychometrika. 1948;13:185-187. Dietterich TG. Approximate statistical tests for comparing supervised classification learning algorithms. Neural Comput. 1998;10(7):1895-1923.

docs.title: delong_test
docs.text:
delong_test(y_true: ArrayLike, y_prob_a: ArrayLike, y_prob_b: ArrayLike, *, pos_label: Any = None, level: float = 0.95) -> TestResult

DeLong's test for two correlated ROC AUCs (same observations, two models). estimate is AUC_A − AUC_B and ci its confidence interval.

Reference: DeLong ER, DeLong DM, Clarke-Pearson DL. Biometrics. 1988;44(3):837-845.

docs.title: paired_bootstrap_test
docs.text:
paired_bootstrap_test(metric: Any, y_true: ArrayLike, y_pred_a: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, y_pred_b: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, *, y_prob_a: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, y_prob_b: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, sample_weight: Optional[ArrayLike] = None, n_resamples: int = 2000, level: float = 0.95, random_state: Optional[int] = None, stratify: Optional[bool] = None, alternative: Literal['two-sided', 'greater', 'less'] = 'two-sided', resampling: str = 'numpy', **metric_kwargs: Any) -> TestResult

Paired bootstrap test for any metric: is metric(A) − metric(B) different from 0?

Both models are evaluated on the same resampled observations. The p-value uses the shifted bootstrap distribution (difference re-centred on 0 under the null), with the +1 correction so it is never 0: p = (1 + #{|δ* − δ̂| ≥ |δ̂|}) / (B + 1) for a two-sided test. ci is the percentile interval of δ*.

resampling="native" (opt-in) draws the resample indices in the compiled core; see :func:bootstrap_ci.

Reference: Efron B, Tibshirani RJ. An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman & Hall; 1993, ch. 16.

docs.title: evalsuite.stats.hypothesis
docs.text:
Hypothesis tests for comparing scores, groups and categorical outcomes.

Each test returns a :class:TestResult with the statistic, p-value, an effect size in estimate (named in params["effect_size"]) and, where standard, a confidence interval. SciPy is the reference: the common tests compute the same statistics directly (one ranking pass, closed-form tails, cached Shapiro–Wilk weights) and are tested to match SciPy, falling back to SciPy where it uses a different algorithm (exact permutation tests, older Shapiro–Wilk); EvalSuite adds input validation, effect sizes and consistent results.

docs.title: t_test
docs.text:
t_test(a: ArrayLike, b: ArrayLike, *, equal_var: bool = False, alternative: Alternative = 'two-sided', level: float = 0.95) -> TestResult

Two-sample t-test for mean(a) − mean(b). Welch's test by default (equal_var=False), which does not assume equal variances; equal_var=True gives Student's test. estimate is the mean difference with a confidence interval; params["cohens_d"] is the standardised effect size.

References: Welch BL. Biometrika. 1947;34(1-2):28-35. Student. Biometrika. 1908;6(1):1-25.

docs.title: paired_t_test
docs.text:
paired_t_test(a: ArrayLike, b: ArrayLike, *, alternative: Alternative = 'two-sided', level: float = 0.95) -> TestResult

Paired t-test for the mean of a − b (for example per-fold scores of two models on the same folds). estimate is the mean difference with a confidence interval; params["cohens_dz"] is d_z.

docs.title: mann_whitney_test
docs.text:
mann_whitney_test(a: ArrayLike, b: ArrayLike, *, alternative: Alternative = 'two-sided') -> TestResult

Mann–Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum) test. statistic is U for a; estimate is the rank-biserial correlation r = 2U/(n₁n₂) − 1 (equal to Cliff's delta), and params["auc"] = U/(n₁n₂) = P(a > b) + ½P(a = b).

References: Mann HB, Whitney DR. Ann Math Stat. 1947;18(1):50-60. Kerby DS. Compr Psychol. 2014;3:11.IT.3.1.

docs.title: wilcoxon_test
docs.text:
wilcoxon_test(a: ArrayLike, b: ArrayLike, *, alternative: Alternative = 'two-sided', zero_method: Literal['wilcox', 'pratt', 'zsplit'] = 'wilcox') -> TestResult

Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired samples (a − b). estimate is the matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation (T⁺ − T⁻) / (T⁺ + T⁻) over the non-zero differences.

Reference: Wilcoxon F. Biometrics Bull. 1945;1(6):80-83.

docs.title: kruskal_wallis_test
docs.text:
kruskal_wallis_test(*groups: ArrayLike) -> TestResult

Kruskal–Wallis H test: do two or more independent groups come from the same distribution? estimate is epsilon-squared, H / ((n² − 1)/(n + 1)).

References: Kruskal WH, Wallis WA. JASA. 1952;47(260):583-621. Tomczak M, Tomczak E. Trends Sport Sci. 2014;1(21):19-25.

docs.title: friedman_test
docs.text:
friedman_test(*groups: ArrayLike) -> TestResult

Friedman test for three or more related samples (for example several models scored on the same datasets or folds; each argument is one model's scores). estimate is Kendall's W = χ² / (n (k − 1)).

References: Friedman M. JASA. 1937;32(200):675-701. Demšar J. Statistical comparisons of classifiers over multiple data sets. JMLR. 2006;7:1-30.

docs.title: shapiro_wilk_test
docs.text:
shapiro_wilk_test(x: ArrayLike) -> TestResult

Shapiro–Wilk test of normality (3 ≤ n ≤ 5000 for an accurate p-value).

Reference: Shapiro SS, Wilk MB. Biometrika. 1965;52(3-4):591-611.

docs.title: chi_square_test
docs.text:
chi_square_test(table: ArrayLike, *, correction: bool = True) -> TestResult

Pearson's χ² test of independence for an r × c contingency table. Yates' continuity correction is applied to 2 × 2 tables unless correction=False. estimate is Cramér's V (from the uncorrected statistic, as in :func:cramers_v); params["expected"] holds the expected counts (the approximation is doubtful when many are below 5).

Reference: Pearson K. Philos Mag. 1900;50(302):157-175. Cramér H. Mathematical Methods of Statistics. 1946.

docs.title: fisher_exact_test
docs.text:
fisher_exact_test(table: ArrayLike, *, alternative: Alternative = 'two-sided') -> TestResult

Fisher's exact test for a 2 × 2 table. estimate is the sample odds ratio (a·d)/(b·c).

Reference: Fisher RA. J R Stat Soc. 1922;85(1):87-94.

docs.title: evalsuite.stats.effect
docs.text: Effect sizes and multiple-comparison correction.

docs.title: cohens_d
docs.text:
cohens_d(a: ArrayLike, b: ArrayLike, *, paired: bool = False) -> float

Cohen's d for mean(a) − mean(b).

Independent samples: difference over the pooled standard deviation. paired=True: mean difference over the standard deviation of the differences (d_z), for per-fold or per-subject scores of two models.

Reference: Cohen J. Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences. 2nd ed. Erlbaum; 1988. Lakens D. Calculating and reporting effect sizes. Front Psychol. 2013;4:863.

docs.title: hedges_g
docs.text:
hedges_g(a: ArrayLike, b: ArrayLike, *, paired: bool = False) -> float

Hedges' g: Cohen's d with the exact small-sample bias correction J(df) = Γ(df/2) / (√(df/2) Γ((df−1)/2)).

Reference: Hedges LV. Distribution theory for Glass's estimator of effect size and related estimators. J Educ Stat. 1981;6(2):107-128.

docs.title: cliffs_delta
docs.text:
cliffs_delta(a: ArrayLike, b: ArrayLike) -> float

Cliff's delta: P(a > b) − P(a < b) over all pairs; a non-parametric effect size in [−1, 1].

Computed in O((n + m) log m). Reference: Cliff N. Dominance statistics: ordinal analyses to answer ordinal questions. Psychol Bull. 1993;114(3):494-509.

docs.title: cramers_v
docs.text:
cramers_v(table: ArrayLike, *, bias_correction: bool = False) -> float

Cramér's V for an r × c contingency table: √(χ² / (n · (min(r, c) − 1))), from the uncorrected Pearson χ². bias_correction=True applies Bergsma's correction, which reduces the upward bias in small samples.

References: Cramér H. Mathematical Methods of Statistics. Princeton; 1946. Bergsma W. A bias-correction for Cramér's V and Tschuprow's T. J Korean Stat Soc. 2013;42(3):323-328.

docs.title: adjust_pvalues
docs.text:
adjust_pvalues(p_values: ArrayLike, *, method: Literal['bonferroni', 'holm', 'hochberg', 'bh', 'by'] = 'holm') -> NDArray[np.float64]

Adjust p-values for multiple comparisons (same order as the input).

"holm" (default; controls the family-wise error rate, uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni), "bonferroni", "hochberg" (step-up; controls the family-wise error rate under independence or positive dependence, more powerful than Holm), "bh" (Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate) or "by" (Benjamini-Yekutieli, FDR under arbitrary dependence).

References: Holm S. Scand J Stat. 1979;6(2):65-70. Hochberg Y. Biometrika. 1988;75(4):800-802. Benjamini Y, Hochberg Y. J R Stat Soc B. 1995;57(1):289-300. Benjamini Y, Yekutieli D. Ann Stat. 2001;29(4):1165-1188.

docs.title: evalsuite.stats.planning
docs.text:
Study planning: how many test items are needed for a given precision or to detect a given difference.

  • :func:sample_size_proportion — items so that a proportion (accuracy, sensitivity, ...) has a confidence interval no wider than ± half_width.
  • :func:sample_size_two_proportions — items to detect a difference between two models' accuracies, on the same items (paired, McNemar; Connor 1987) or on separate samples (Fleiss, Levin & Paik 2003).
  • :func:sample_size_auc — positives and negatives for an ROC AUC interval of given width, or to show an AUC above a reference value (Hanley & McNeil 1982; Obuchowski 1998).
  • :func:sample_size_mean_difference — pairs (or per-group observations) to detect a difference in a mean score or loss (paired or two-sample t approximation).
  • power_* counterparts give the power achieved with a fixed sample.

All formulas are the standard normal-approximation ones and are documented with their references; sample sizes are rounded up.

docs.title: SampleSize dataclass
docs.text: A planned sample size with the assumptions behind it.

docs.title: sample_size_proportion
docs.text:
sample_size_proportion(p: float, half_width: float, *, level: float = 0.95) -> SampleSize

Items so that a proportion near p is estimated within ± half_width (normal approximation, n = z² p (1 − p) / w²). Use p = 0.5 when nothing is known (the most conservative choice).

docs.title: sample_size_two_proportions
docs.text:
sample_size_two_proportions(p1: float, p2: float, *, alpha: float = 0.05, power: float = 0.8, paired: bool = True, discordance: Optional[float] = None, two_sided: bool = True) -> SampleSize

Items needed to detect accuracy p1 vs p2.

paired=True (default; both models answer the same items, McNemar's test, Connor 1987): n = (z_α √ψ + z_β √(ψ − δ²))² / δ², with ψ the share of items the models disagree on (discordance). Without discordance, ψ assumes independent errors, p1(1 − p2) + p2(1 − p1), which is conservative when the models are correlated (they usually are; a pilot estimate of ψ gives a smaller n). paired=False: two separate samples, n per group (Fleiss, Levin & Paik 2003).

docs.title: power_two_proportions
docs.text:
power_two_proportions(n: int, p1: float, p2: float, *, alpha: float = 0.05, paired: bool = True, discordance: Optional[float] = None, two_sided: bool = True) -> float

Power to detect p1 vs p2 with n items (paired) or n per group (unpaired).

docs.title: sample_size_auc
docs.text:
sample_size_auc(auc: float, *, prevalence: float, half_width: Optional[float] = None, auc0: Optional[float] = None, level: float = 0.95, alpha: float = 0.05, power: float = 0.8) -> SampleSize

Total items (positives + negatives at prevalence) for an ROC AUC near auc.

Give half_width for an interval no wider than ± half_width, or auc0 to show that the AUC exceeds a reference value (one-sided, at alpha with power; variance under both hypotheses, Obuchowski 1998). Variances follow Hanley & McNeil (1982).

docs.title: power_auc
docs.text:
power_auc(n: int, auc: float, auc0: float, *, prevalence: float, alpha: float = 0.05) -> float

Power of a one-sided test that the AUC exceeds auc0 with n items at prevalence.

docs.title: sample_size_mean_difference
docs.text:
sample_size_mean_difference(delta: float, sd: float, *, alpha: float = 0.05, power: float = 0.8, paired: bool = True, two_sided: bool = True) -> SampleSize

Items to detect a difference delta in a mean score (a loss, a rating, a per-item metric).

paired=True: sd is the standard deviation of the per-item differences; n = ((z_α + z_β) σ / δ)², refined with the t distribution. paired=False: sd is the per-group standard deviation; n per group = 2 ((z_α + z_β) σ / δ)², refined likewise.

docs.title: power_mean_difference
docs.text:
power_mean_difference(n: int, delta: float, sd: float, *, alpha: float = 0.05, paired: bool = True, two_sided: bool = True) -> float

Power of a paired (or two-sample, n per group) t-test to detect delta (noncentral t).

docs.title: evalsuite.data_quality
docs.text:
Data quality before evaluation: leakage between splits, likely label errors, and a summary card of a data set.

import evalsuite as es es.leakage_report(train_df, test_df, target="label", id_column="patient_id") es.label_issues(y, pred_probs) # likely mislabelled examples (confident learning) es.dataset_card(test_df, target="label", groups=["sex", "site"])

leakage_report finds test rows that also appear in training (exact duplicates after normalising numbers and text), near-duplicates (numeric rows within near_tol standardised units of a training row; texts whose word-shingle Jaccard similarity is at least text_threshold, found with MinHash), shared identifiers (the same patient or document in both splits) and features that predict the target almost perfectly (a sign that the answer leaked into the inputs). label_issues implements confident learning (Northcutt, Jiang & Chuang 2021): an example is flagged when its out-of-sample probability for another class clears that class's average self-confidence threshold. dataset_card summarises size, missing values, class balance, feature types, subgroup counts and duplicates.

docs.title: LeakageReport dataclass
docs.text: Overlap between a training and a test set. findings lists each check with the affected test rows.

docs.title: leaked_rows property
docs.text:
leaked_rows: list[int]

Test rows affected by any duplicate or shared-identifier finding (sorted).

docs.title: LabelIssues dataclass
docs.text: Examples whose given label looks wrong, ranked by how unlikely the label is under the model.

docs.title: DatasetCard dataclass
docs.text: A summary of a data set for a paper's methods section or a model card.

docs.title: leakage_report
docs.text:
leakage_report(train: Any, test: Any, *, target: Optional[str] = None, id_column: Optional[str] = None, text_columns: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, columns: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, near_tol: float = 0.001, text_threshold: float = 0.8, shingle: int = 3, target_auc: float = 0.99) -> LeakageReport

Check a train / test split for leakage (see the module docstring). columns restricts the feature columns compared (default: all shared columns except target and id_column).

docs.title: label_issues
docs.text:
label_issues(y: Any, pred_probs: Any, *, classes: Any = None) -> LabelIssues

Likely label errors by confident learning (Northcutt et al. 2021). pred_probs must be out-of-sample (e.g. cross-validated) class probabilities, n × k; columns are integer labels, or classes= gives the label of each column. Returned examples are sorted from the most to the least suspicious.

docs.title: dataset_card
docs.text:
dataset_card(data: Any, *, target: Optional[str] = None, groups: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None) -> DatasetCard

Size, column types, missing values, numeric summaries, class balance of target, counts per subgroup (groups) and duplicate rows.

docs.title: evalsuite.drift
docs.text:
Data drift between a reference set (training or validation data) and current data, feature by feature.

import evalsuite as es rep = es.drift_report(train_df, live_df) # DataFrames, dicts of columns or 2-D arrays rep.drifted() # features that changed significantly and materially print(rep.summary()); rep.to_html()

Numeric features: two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, population stability index (PSI, reference-quantile bins) and Wasserstein distance in reference standard deviations. Categorical features (strings, booleans, or categorical=[...]): chi-square test of homogeneity, PSI over categories and Jensen–Shannon distance. Missing-value rates are compared with a two-proportion z-test. P-values are Holm-adjusted across features. A feature is flagged when its adjusted p-value is below alpha and the shift is material (PSI ≥ psi_threshold or distance ≥ distance_threshold: 0.1 reference SDs, or a Jensen–Shannon distance of 0.1), so a large data set does not flag trivial shifts; a significant change of at least one point in the missing-value rate is flagged too. Model scores and labels can be checked the same way (es.drift_report({"score": ref_scores}, {"score": live_scores})).

docs.title: DriftReport dataclass
docs.text: Per-feature drift results. features rows carry the test, statistic, raw and Holm-adjusted p-values, PSI, a distance, missing-rate change and whether the feature drifted.

docs.title: drifted
docs.text:
drifted() -> list[str]

Names of the drifted features, largest PSI first.

docs.title: drift_report
docs.text:
drift_report(reference: Any, current: Any, *, features: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, categorical: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, alpha: float = 0.05, psi_threshold: float = 0.1, distance_threshold: float = 0.1, bins: int = 10, eps: float = 0.0001) -> DriftReport

Compare every shared feature of reference and current (see the module docstring). features selects and orders features (or names the columns of 2-D arrays); categorical forces features to be treated as categories (for example integer codes).

docs.title: evalsuite.forecasting
docs.text:
Forecast evaluation: scaled errors, quantile and interval scores, CRPS, and the Diebold–Mariano test.

import evalsuite as es es.mase(y_test, y_hat, y_train=y_train, m=12) # < 1: better than the seasonal naive forecast es.interval_score(y_test, lower, upper, level=0.9) # width plus penalties for misses es.crps(y_test, ensemble=samples) # or crps(y_test, mean=mu, sd=sigma) es.diebold_mariano(y_test, y_hat_a, y_hat_b, h=1) # are A's forecasts more accurate than B's? es.forecast_report(y_test, {"ets": a, "arima": b}, y_train=y_train, m=12)

Definitions: MASE and RMSSE follow Hyndman & Koehler (2006) and the M5 competition, scaled by the in-sample (seasonal) naive forecast; the interval score and MSIS follow Gneiting & Raftery (2007) and the M4 competition; CRPS for ensembles uses the energy form (as properscoring) and for normal forecasts the closed form; the Diebold–Mariano (1995) test uses the Harvey, Leybourne & Newbold (1997) small-sample correction with a t reference distribution.

docs.title: ForecastReport dataclass
docs.text: Accuracy of several forecasts of one series, with Diebold–Mariano tests against a baseline.

docs.title: to_html
docs.text:
to_html(*, digits: int = 3) -> str

The Markdown tables as an HTML fragment (escaped), e.g. for :func:evalsuite.html_report.

docs.title: mase
docs.text:
mase(y_true: Any, y_pred: Any, *, y_train: Any, m: int = 1) -> MetricResult

Mean absolute scaled error: MAE divided by the in-sample MAE of the seasonal naive forecast with period m (1 for the plain random walk). Below 1 beats the naive forecast.

docs.title: rmsse
docs.text:
rmsse(y_true: Any, y_pred: Any, *, y_train: Any, m: int = 1) -> MetricResult

Root mean squared scaled error (M5 competition): sqrt(MSE / in-sample MSE of the seasonal naive forecast).

docs.title: pinball_loss
docs.text:
pinball_loss(y_true: Any, quantile_preds: Any, *, quantiles: Any) -> MetricResult

Mean pinball (quantile) loss. quantile_preds is n × q (one column per quantile in quantiles) or a vector for a single quantile. params["per_quantile"] holds each quantile's loss (as scikit-learn's mean_pinball_loss); the value is their mean.

docs.title: interval_score
docs.text:
interval_score(y_true: Any, lower: Any, upper: Any, *, level: float = 0.95) -> MetricResult

Mean interval (Winkler) score of central level prediction intervals (Gneiting & Raftery 2007): width + (2/α)·(lower − y) when y < lower + (2/α)·(y − upper) when y > upper, α = 1 − level. Lower is better.

docs.title: msis
docs.text:
msis(y_true: Any, lower: Any, upper: Any, *, y_train: Any, m: int = 1, level: float = 0.95) -> MetricResult

Mean scaled interval score (M4 competition): the interval score divided by the in-sample MAE of the seasonal naive forecast.

docs.title: interval_coverage
docs.text:
interval_coverage(y_true: Any, lower: Any, upper: Any, *, level: Optional[float] = None) -> MetricResult

Share of observations inside their prediction intervals, with a Wilson interval; with the nominal level the binomial test of coverage = level is added (params["p_value"]).

docs.title: crps
docs.text:
crps(y_true: Any, *, ensemble: Any = None, mean: Any = None, sd: Any = None) -> MetricResult

Mean continuous ranked probability score. Give ensemble (n × m sample paths / members) for the empirical CRPS E|X − y| − ½E|X − X'|, or mean and sd for normal forecasts (closed form). Lower is better; for a point forecast it reduces to the absolute error.

docs.title: diebold_mariano
docs.text:
diebold_mariano(y_true: Any, pred_a: Any, pred_b: Any, *, h: int = 1, loss: str = 'squared', alternative: str = 'two-sided', harvey: bool = True) -> MetricResult

Diebold–Mariano test of equal predictive accuracy of two forecasts of the same series. loss is "squared" or "absolute"; h is the forecast horizon (the loss differential's autocorrelation is allowed up to lag h − 1). The value is the DM statistic (negative: A's losses are smaller); params holds the p-value and the mean loss difference. alternative="less" tests that A is more accurate.

docs.title: forecast_report
docs.text:
forecast_report(y_true: Any, forecasts: Mapping[str, Any], *, y_train: Any = None, m: int = 1, baseline: Optional[str] = None, h: int = 1, loss: str = 'squared') -> ForecastReport

MAE, RMSE, sMAPE (and MASE with y_train) for each forecast, and a Holm-adjusted Diebold–Mariano test of each against baseline (the first forecast by default).

docs.title: evalsuite.multilabel
docs.text:
Multi-label classification and ranked retrieval / recommendation reports, with confidence intervals.

import evalsuite as es es.multilabel_report(Y_true, Y_pred, Y_score) # n × labels 0/1 matrices (+ scores for ranking metrics) es.ranking_report(qrels, {"bm25": run_a, "dense": run_b}, k=10)

import evalsuite as es runs = es.run_model(prompts, "openai:gpt-4o-mini") # or "anthropic:claude-…", or any callable es.agent_report(episodes) # success, steps, tool use, cost, with CIs es.conversation_report(dialogues) # per-turn and per-dialogue scores es.cost_quality_report({"a": runs_a, "b": runs_b}) # quality, cost and latency per model es.contamination_check(benchmark_items, training_texts) # n-gram overlap with training data

run_model calls the provider's official SDK (pip install openai / anthropic; keys come from the usual environment variables and are never stored) or any Python callable, with retries, a small thread pool and an on-disk cache in EvalSuite's cache folder (evalsuite cache info), so re-running an evaluation costs nothing. Responses record latency and token counts for cost reports. Intervals in the reports are Wilson intervals for rates and cluster-bootstrap percentile intervals (by dialogue / episode) for means.

docs.title: evalsuite.judging
docs.text:
LLM-as-judge evaluation in one report: who wins, and whether the judge can be trusted.

judge_report(records) takes pairwise judgements (one record per comparison) and returns:

  • Win rates of every model with Wilson intervals, the pairwise win matrix and Bradley–Terry ratings with bootstrap intervals (comparisons resampled).
  • Position bias: how often the verdict survives swapping the order (verdict_swapped), and whether the inconsistent verdicts favour the response shown first (two-sided binomial test).
  • Length bias: how often the longer response wins decisive comparisons (binomial test against 0.5).
  • Self-preference: when the judge is itself one of the models (judge), how much more often it picks its own outputs than other judges or humans do on the same comparisons.
  • Agreement with humans (human verdicts): raw agreement (Wilson) and Cohen's kappa (bootstrap interval).

rubric_report(records) summarises rubric scores (one record per item × criterion × model, optionally per rater): the mean per model and criterion with t intervals, inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's alpha) and correlation with human scores.

Every bias is reported with its test and is flagged only when significant, so a report does not cry wolf on small samples.

docs.title: evalsuite.rag_report
docs.text:
End-to-end RAG evaluation: retrieval, grounding and answer quality in one report, with every failure traced to the stage that caused it.

rag_report(records, k=5) takes one record per question:

  • retrieved — ranked document ids; relevant — the ids that answer the question (optional);
  • answer — the system's answer; reference — the gold answer (a string or a list of acceptable answers);
  • grounded (true / false) or support (per-claim 0 / 1 or scores in [0, 1], e.g. from an NLI model or an LLM judge) — whether the answer is supported by the retrieved context (optional).

It reports hit rate, recall and MRR at k, exact match and token F1, the grounded rate, each with an interval, and classifies every question:

  • correct — right answer, supported by the context (or no grounding data given);
  • retrieval_failure — wrong answer and no relevant document in the top k: fix the retriever;
  • generation_failure — wrong answer although a relevant document was retrieved: fix the prompt / model;
  • unsupported_correct — right answer that the context does not support (memorised or lucky);
  • wrong_unknown_cause — wrong answer without relevance labels to tell retrieval from generation.

The breakdown (with Wilson intervals) says where to invest, and examples lists the ids in each class.

Datasets are downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub by the optional datasets package and are never bundled. Runs that already contain reference (or correct) need no download at all.

HumanEval completions must be executed to be scored. EvalSuite never runs model-generated code: run them in your own sandbox (for example the official human-eval harness) and pass passed (true / false) per item, or n_samples and n_correct for an unbiased pass@k estimate.

docs.title: evalsuite.harness
docs.text:
A statistically careful LLM evaluation harness.

Point it at each model's outputs (JSONL files, lists of records or DataFrames) and it scores them, puts an interval on every number and only ranks models apart when the difference is significant:

  • every model's score with a Wilson (or bootstrap) confidence interval;
  • paired tests between models on the items they share (exact McNemar for correct / incorrect, a paired bootstrap for graded scores), with Holm-adjusted p-values;
  • rank groups: a model's rank is 1 + the number of models significantly better than it, so statistical ties share a rank;
  • per-category breakdowns with intervals;
  • checks: unmatched or missing items, extraction failures, contamination (n-gram overlap of each item with a training corpus you provide, and scores on clean versus overlapping items), and judge position bias when the records carry verdicts in both presentation orders.

Each record is a mapping with an id and either a correct / score value from your own grader, or a prediction (model output) scored against the reference (gold answer) with scorer. Optional fields: category, prompt (for the contamination check), verdict and verdict_swapped (judge verdicts "A" / "B" / "tie" with the two answers in the original and the swapped order).

import evalsuite as es runs = { ... "model-a": [{"id": i, "prediction": "4", "reference": "4"} for i in range(30)], ... "model-b": [{"id": i, "prediction": "4" if i % 3 else "5", "reference": "4"} for i in range(30)], ... } lb = es.leaderboard(runs, scorer="exact_match") best = lb.rows[0] best.get("model"), best.get("rank") ('model-a', 1)

leaderboard(runs: Mapping[str, Records], *, scorer: Optional[Union[str, Callable[[str, str], Any]]] = None, references: Optional[Records] = None, benchmark: Optional[str] = None, level: float = 0.95, alpha: float = 0.05, correction: str = 'holm', train_corpus: Optional[Iterable[str]] = None, ngram: int = 13, n_resamples: int = 2000, random_state: Optional[int] = 0) -> Leaderboard

Score several models' outputs and rank them with intervals and paired tests (see the module docs).

runs maps model names to records (a JSONL / JSON path, a list of dicts or a DataFrame). references optionally supplies the gold answers separately (records with id and reference). scorer is one of "exact_match" (SQuAD-normalised), "contains", "gsm8k", "boxed", "choice", "last_line", "numeric", or a callable (prediction, reference) -> score in [0, 1]; records with a correct or score field are used as given. train_corpus (iterable of texts) enables the contamination check. benchmark ("gsm8k", "mmlu", "arc", "arc-easy", "truthfulqa", "humaneval") picks that benchmark's scorer (unless scorer is given); pass references=es.load_benchmark(name) for its gold answers and categories. For HumanEval, records carry passed (or n_samples / n_correct) from your own sandboxed execution; the score is pass@1.

docs.title: evalsuite.auto_report
docs.text:
One call (or one command) from a table of predictions to a full HTML evaluation report.

import evalsuite as es es.auto_report("predictions.csv") # works out the columns and the task es.auto_report(df, target="label", prob="risk", groups=["sex"], path="report.html")

From the shell: evalsuite report predictions.csv writes report.html next to the data.

Columns are recognised by name (case-insensitive): the outcome (y_true, label, target, outcome, truth, actual, y), predicted labels or values (y_pred, pred, prediction, predicted), predicted probabilities (y_prob, prob, proba, probability, risk, score, or one prob_<class> column per class), subgroups (sex, gender, age_group, race, ethnicity, site, group) and clusters (patient_id, subject_id, cluster). Anything detected wrongly can be given explicitly. The task follows from the outcome: two classes → binary (discrimination, calibration, TRIPOD+AI card, fairness when groups exist), more classes → multiclass, otherwise regression.

docs.text:
One self-contained HTML file for a whole evaluation: tables, intervals, plots and narrative, to attach to a paper, a pull request or an e-mail.

page = es.html_report( ... {"Test set": result, "Leaderboard": board, "Fairness": fairness, "Calibration": es.plot.calibration(...)}, ... title="Sepsis model v3 evaluation", path="report.html", ... )

Each section can be any EvalSuite result (evaluate, compare, leaderboard, report_card, fairness_report, judge_report, rag_report, sample-size plans, metric results), a Matplotlib figure (embedded as a PNG), or text (paragraphs; Markdown tables are rendered as tables). The file has inline CSS, no scripts and no external requests, so it opens anywhere and is safe to share; all text is escaped.

docs.title: evalsuite.workflow
docs.text:
Workflow integrations: log results to MLflow or Weights & Biases, keep a history of evaluations and flag regressions, and serve EvalSuite over HTTP.

import evalsuite as es es.log_to_mlflow(result) # inside an active MLflow run (or pass run_id=) es.log_to_wandb(result) # inside wandb.init() es.record_history(result, model="v3", dataset="test-2024") # appends to .evalsuite/history.jsonl es.check_regression(result, model="v3", dataset="test-2024") # against the latest recorded result

Logging writes each metric's value and interval bounds as scalar metrics (accuracy, accuracy_ci_low, …), the full result as JSON, and its HTML table, so dashboards show intervals rather than bare numbers. The history is a plain JSON-lines file (one evaluation per line) that can live in the repository next to the code.

docs.text:
EvalSuite's cache folder: where downloaded benchmark data and the update-check record live.

import evalsuite as es es.cache_info() # location, size, entries es.clear_cache(older_than="30d") # or clear_cache() for everything

The folder is $EVALSUITE_CACHE if set, else $XDG_CACHE_HOME/evalsuite, %LOCALAPPDATA%\evalsuite on Windows, or ~/.cache/evalsuite. From the command line: evalsuite cache info and evalsuite cache clear.

Automatic clearing: at most once a day, in the background after import, entries not used for EVALSUITE_CACHE_MAX_AGE (default 90 days) are removed, then the least recently used entries until the cache is below EVALSUITE_CACHE_MAX_SIZE (default 2 GB). Set EVALSUITE_CACHE_AUTO_CLEAN=0 to turn it off. Only folders EvalSuite created (they carry a marker file) are ever touched, and only whole entries (one data set download, one record) are removed, never part of one.
